blocks.text: India replaced its colonial criminal laws with three new legislations:
1) Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 > Replaced IPC, 1860.
2) Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 —> Replaced CrPC, 1973.
3) Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023 — Replaced Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
All three laws came into force on Ist July 2024.
1. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023
Replaced IPC, 1860.
Contains 358 Sections (earlier 511 in IPC).
Defines gender inclusively (male, female, transgender).
Bharatiya Nyaya Samhita (BNS), 2023 deals with criminal substantive law, i.e., definition of offences and their punishments.
BNS promotes digital reforms like virtual court hearings to modernize the justice system.
Organized crime involves serious large-scale offences like terror, drug trafficking,while petty organized crime includes small-scale group crimes like theft and snatching.
Key Changes & New Offence:

Introduces: Mob lynching, Organised crime, Terrorism, False promise of marriage; Attempt to suicide treated diffe- rently (humanitarian approach); Community service intro- duced as punishment for minor offences.
Sedition (Section 124A IPC) removed and replaced by: Section 152 — Acts endangering sovereignty, unity & integrity of India.
Section 2 > Gender definition (inclusive)
Other removals: Adultery, Section 377 (partially removed contextually), Obsolete offences.
Mob lynching (death) > Death penalty or life imprisonment
Defamation — Imprisonment + fine + community service option
Graded punishment system introduced
Important Concepts: Abetment: Includes aiding, instigating, or counselling
Child: Below 18 years
Organised crime: Crime committed by a crime syndicate
Focus on: National security, Victim-centric justice, Modern crimes (cyber, organised crime)
Section 106(1): General negligent death — up to 5 years imprisonment.
Section 106(2): Hit and run causing death — up to 10 years imprisonment + fine (if the driver flees without reporting)
2. Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023
Replaces Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Contains 170 Sections
Digital evidence = Primary evidence (at par)
Governs evidence and proof in courts
The BSA 2023 modernizes evidence law by recognizing electronic and digital records. For this, it aligns with the Information Technology Act, 2000, which already provides:
Legal recognition of electronic records.

A confession made to a police officer is inadmissible in court. Section 23 of the BSA emphasizes that only voluntary confessions free from coercion, threat or inducement are admissible as evidence in court.
Under BSA, secondary evidence (such as photocopies or lost, destroyed or otherwise unavailable for valid reasons.
Key Changes:
Electronic evidence = Same value as paper documents
Digital evidence treated at par with primary evidence
Oral evidence allowed electronically
Introduction of joint trials
Only admissible evidence allowed
Police confession valid only before Magistrate Issues:
Risk of tampering with digital evidence
Certification rules may create contradictions 3. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023
Replaces CrPC, 1973
Contains 531 Sections
Zero FIR — Can be filed at any police station e e-FIR allowed (within 3 days)
Accused must be informed of grounds of arrest imme- diately.
Charges framed within > 60 days (Session Court)
Medical report (rape victim) > within 7 days
BNSS ensures access to FIR through CCTNS (Crime and Criminal Tracking Network & Systems) portal.

Higher courts can grant bail in general, but default bail (is granted when the investigation is not completed within the prescribed time limit usually 60 or 90 days) specifically originates at the Magistrate level.
Important Sections Of BNSS
Section 35 — Arrest without a warrant or magistrate order.
Section 38 > Gives arrested person right to meet an advocate during interrogation.
Section 47 > Arrested person must be informed of grounds of arrest and right to bail.
Section 50 > This section empowers a police officer or any person making an arrest to seize any offensive weapons found on the arrested person.
Section 58 — No detention beyond 24 hours without Magistrate's approval.
Section 62 > It mandates that no arrest shall be made except in accordance with the provisions of the BNSS or any other law currently in force providing for arrest.
Section 105 — The process of search and seizures be recorded through Audio-video electronic means.
Section 173 — Allows the registration of an electronic FIR (e-FIR).
Section 479 + Maximum detention period (maximum period of imprisonment specified for the alleged offense under the law) for undertrial prisoners.
Section 481 — Bail to require accused to appear before next Appellate court.
Section 482 — Governs Anticipatory Bail (pre-arrest) or non-bailable offences.
Section 530 — All the trials and proceedings under the sanhita may be conducted in electronic mode.
Investigation Reforms:
Forensic investigation mandatory (27 years punishment cases)
Videography of search & seizure compulsory
Voice samples allowed as evidence
Victims have Right to: Chargesheet copy, Case updates, Witness protection.
Police custody up to 15 days (within 40-60 days window)
Community service recognised
Trial in absentia allowed
Overall Significance of New Laws:
1) Shift from colonial + modern justice system 2) Focus on: Digitalisation, Speedy justice, Victim rights, National security.
BNS — Defines crimes & punishments
BNSS — Defines procedure (FIR, arrest, trial)
BSA — Defines evidence & proof
